script.title: Why New Zealand Set Stoats Loose on the Kiwi
script.hook: New Zealand released stoats to kill its rabbits, and the stoats turned on the kiwi instead.
script._cold_open: Deep in a forest where no rabbit lives, a stoat crouches over a bird's egg and a poorly flighted chick.

_hook_contract.viewer_question: Why did New Zealand deliberately release stoats, and what happened to the kiwi?
_hook_contract.supported_answer: Officials released stoats to control rabbits, but stoats spread into forests without rabbits and became the greatest killer of kiwi chicks.
_hook_contract.contrast: Intended to control rabbits; instead decimated native birds including kiwi chicks.
_hook_contract.callback_image: a stoat standing over a bird's egg in the forest
_hook_contract.closing_question: When you import a predator to solve one problem, who decides what else it is allowed to eat?

scenes.narration: New Zealand released stoats to kill its rabbits, and the stoats turned on the kiwi instead. Deep in a forest where no rabbit lives, a stoat crouches over a bird's egg and a poorly flighted chick. New Zealand's rabbits bred without limit, stripping pasture bare, so farmers trusted a tidy 19th-century idea: nature balances itself.

claim_refs.narration_phrase: New Zealand's rabbits bred without limit, stripping pasture bare, so farmers trusted a tidy 19th-century idea: nature balances itself.
Deep in a forest where no rabbit lives, a stoat crouches over a bird's egg and a poorly flighted chick.

event.text: New Zealand's rabbit population was self-sustaining, and the idea of bringing in stoats to control it rested on a naive 19th-century notion of the balance of nature.

scenes.narration: Ornithologists protested loudly. Officials ignored them, and in 1884 opened the crates and let the stoats run free.

event.text: Despite protests from ornithologists, stoats were imported and released in 1884 to control the rabbits.

scenes.narration: And it worked, at first. The stoats hunted the rabbits they were brought to control, exactly the job intended.

event.text: The stoats were introduced in the hope of bringing the country's rabbit population under control, the task they were meant for.

scenes.narration: No rabbit ever taught these forests to fear a stoat.

claim_refs.narration_phrase: No rabbit ever taught these forests to fear a stoat.

scenes.narration: A stoat does not read a farmer's plan. It followed its hunger past the pastures, into the forests where no rabbit lived at all.

event.text: After release, stoats quickly spread to forests and other areas where there were no rabbits, and fed on poorly flighted birds and their eggs.

scenes.narration: There it found poorly flighted birds that could barely lift off the ground, and clutches of eggs left warm and unwatched. Easy meals. Nothing fought back.

scenes.narration: No bird was more defenceless than the kiwi: flightless, nesting on bare ground, raising a chick with no way to run.

claim_refs.narration_phrase: No bird was more defenceless than the kiwi: flightless, nesting on bare ground, raising a chick with no way to run.

event.text: Stoats have been identified as the greatest threat to juvenile kiwi, killing an estimated 60% of chicks born in the wild.

scenes.narration: So the stoat became the chicks' deadliest enemy. Of every ten kiwi chicks hatched in the wild, six are killed before they ever grow up.

scenes.narration: At Riponui Reserve, 2002 looked like a triumph: six tagged chicks tracked, and every single one survived its first vulnerable months.

claim_refs.narration_phrase: At Riponui Reserve, 2002 looked like a triumph: six tagged chicks tracked, and every single one survived its first vulnerable months.

event.text: At Riponui Reserve, kiwi chick survival dropped from a peak of 100% of 6 chicks radio-tagged in 2002 to 0% of 15 chicks monitored between 2005 and 2008.

scenes.narration: Then came the years between 2005 and 2008. Fifteen chicks were monitored across that stretch. Not one survived. The reserve went silent.

event.text: At Riponui Reserve, kiwi chick survival dropped from a peak of 100% of 6 chicks radio-tagged in 2002 to 0% of 15 chicks monitored between 2005 and 2008.

scenes.narration: Leave the fences off entirely, and the picture turns bleak. In unmanaged forest, barely five chicks in a hundred ever make it to adulthood.

event.text: At unmanaged sites, high stoat predation can reduce kiwi recruitment to 5%, compared with the roughly 20% recruitment typically required to maintain a stable population.

scenes.narration: To hold steady, a kiwi population needs about one chick in five to survive. Five in a hundred is a slow unwinding. Every generation, fewer. Then fewer still.

event.text: At unmanaged sites, high stoat predation can reduce kiwi recruitment to 5%, compared with the roughly 20% recruitment typically required to maintain a stable population.

scenes.narration: So the fix now needs a fix. In the forests around Lake Waikaremoana, saving kiwi means hunting the hunter: steel Fenn traps, set in the undergrowth to catch the stoats one by one.

event.text: In the Waikaremoana kiwi project the core intervention is control of predators, primarily stoats, by trapping them in covered Fenn traps baited with white hens' eggs.

scenes.narration: The forest can no longer balance itself. A pale egg, laid as bait, waits in the dark for the predator a nation once invited in. There is no end date on this.

scenes.narration: New Zealand is not alone in this. Cross the Pacific to the island of Guam, where a predator also arrived by accident, and the same story plays out on different wings.

event.text: On Guam, of 12 species of native forest birds present before the brown tree snake, 10 are now extinct on the island and the other two have fewer than 200 individuals.

scenes.narration: Before the brown tree snake slipped ashore, twelve native forest birds sang over Guam. Ten are now gone from the island entirely. The last two cling on, fewer than two hundred birds each.

scenes.narration: Return to where it started: a stoat crouched over a bird's egg in the forest. It is only doing what its hunger tells it. The forest around it is still being defended, trap by trap.
So here is the question to carry out of these woods. When you bring in a predator to solve one problem, who decides what else it is allowed to eat?
